rv.q: It's an utterly (but not fussily) democratic show where everyone gets their moment in the sun and all dignity is sacrificed in favour of laughs.
Buy That Goes Wrong tickets in expectation of giant belly laughs, and you won’t be disappointed.
Yet, along with the rest of the enthusiastic audience, I laughed continually.
Yet watching this tragedy evolve is like seeing a fragile object slip from a high ledge and being unable to interrupt its fall.
Yet, for all the on-stage energy, for all the good wheezes in the script...it has a fatal lack of tension.
It should leave you wanting more; this left me wanting a bit less.

Alun Hood thought the show brought the same “riotous laughs and cosy familiarity” as its predecessors, and “relentlessly hurls every Yuletide trope at us”. “Even the deliberately tackier elements of Libby Todd’s sets and Roberto Surace’s costumes have a satisfyingly glossy sheen, all gorgeously lit by David Howe,” he wrote.
That said, this is largely a joyous show.

This is undiluted, unapologetic sketch theatre, very well done in its way, slightly old-fashioned in thinking itself funnier than it really is, but surprisingly clever in making what is essentially one idea stretch across two hours.
While there are plenty of laughs to be had at That Goes Wrong, the enjoyment comes primarily from an appreciation of the comedic skills on display.
